issues.legal_issue: A summary claim for recovery after unlawful dispossession is determined by possession and unlawful dispossession, independently of the parties’ competing claims to title.
material_facts: The claimant brought a summary suit for possession, alleging that it had been forcibly dispossessed within the period allowed for filing such a suit.
The opposing party relied on competing sale, lease, and agreement claims and challenged the claimant’s sale deed and revenue entries.
The courts found that the claimant had possessed the disputed portion and had been unlawfully dispossessed.
issues.conclusion: The validity of the competing title claims and revenue entries was not relevant to deciding who possessed the property on the relevant date; the summary suit was confined to possession and unlawful dispossession.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 6(1), 6(2), and 6(4) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a person unlawfully dispossessed of immovable property may seek recovery in a summary suit filed within the prescribed period, without adjudication of title; an unsuccessful party may bring a separate suit based on title. Section 6(3) bars appeal and review from a decree or order under the section. The Court relied on Lallu Yashwant Singh (dead) by his LRs. v. Rao Jagdish Singh, Krishna Ram Mahale (D) by LRs v. Mrs. Shobha Venkat Rao, and Sanjay Kumar Pandey v. Gulabahar Sheikh, including the latter’s explanation that revision is available only exceptionally under the settled parameters of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.summary_possession_recovery_case: A person brought a summary proceeding to recover immovable property after alleged dispossession.
predicates.unlawful_dispossession_alleged: The claimant alleged that the opposing party unlawfully dispossessed the claimant from the property.

issues.definition: When a person brings a summary proceeding after alleging unlawful dispossession, the decision determines possession and unlawful dispossession without determining title.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a formal partition does not prevent a court from deciding possession of a specific portion in a summary possession suit when the evidence permits that determination.
material_facts: The land was held by co-sharers, and the opposing party argued that no formal partition had assigned the disputed portion to the claimant’s sellers.
The evidence supported a mutual understanding among the co-sharers about possession of particular portions of the land.
The trial court could determine possession from the revenue records, the police report, and the other evidence on record.
issues.conclusion: The possession issue was capable of determination despite the absence of a formal partition, and the courts did not err by deciding it in the summary suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 calls for a summary determination of possession and unlawful dispossession, not title. The inquiry may proceed where the evidence enables the court to decide possession; the Court found that a mutual understanding among the co-sharers about possession of specific areas was established.

predicates.summary_possession_recovery_case: A person brought a summary proceeding to recover immovable property after alleged dispossession.
predicates.specific_portion_possession_disputed: The parties disputed who possessed a particular portion of land held by co-sharers.
predicates.evidence_supports_possession_finding: The evidence, including records or reports concerning the land, permits a finding about possession of the disputed portion.

issues.definition: If a summary possession proceeding concerns possession of a particular portion and the evidence permits a finding, the court may decide possession despite the absence of formal partition.

issues.legal_issue: In a civil dispute about possession, the court may determine which party possessed the property by weighing the parties’ competing claims on a preponderance of probabilities.
material_facts: The parties made competing claims about possession of the disputed portion.
The opposing party claimed to possess the whole land but had not proved documents relied on to establish that possession.
The opposing party’s earlier suits seeking possession and an injunction supported the conclusion that it was not in possession of the disputed portion.
The trial court concluded that the claimant possessed the disputed portion and had been dispossessed.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was entitled to weigh the competing claims on a preponderance of probabilities, and its conclusion that the opposing party was not in possession was a necessary part of deciding the possession question.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that civil issues are decided by balancing the parties’ claims and counterclaims on a preponderance of probabilities. In a Section 6 Specific Relief Act, 1963 suit, possession and unlawful dispossession are the relevant questions; the court may reach the necessary conclusion about one party’s non-possession to answer who possessed the property.

predicates.civil_possession_dispute: A civil proceeding required the court to decide who possessed immovable property.
predicates.competing_possession_claims: The parties made conflicting claims that each possessed the disputed property.

issues.definition: When a civil proceeding requires a decision about possession and the parties make competing possession claims, the court determines possession by weighing those claims on a preponderance of probabilities.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings on possession that are supported by the evidence do not warrant interference when no basis for disturbing them is shown.
material_facts: The trial court found that the claimant possessed the disputed portion and was unlawfully dispossessed.
The revisional court and the High Court affirmed those findings.
The findings were based on evidence and materials adduced by the parties, including records and reports concerning possession.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no reason to disturb the concurrent findings, affirmed them, and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the concurrent findings as findings of fact reached on the evidence and materials adduced by the parties, and found no reason to interfere. It also noted that Section 6(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 excludes appeal and review from decrees or orders under that section, while the revisional remedy is exceptional under the settled parameters of Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.appeal_against_concurrent_possession_fin: A party appealed from concurrent lower-court findings about possession.
predicates.findings_based_on_evidence: The lower courts reached their possession findings on evidence and materials presented by the parties.
predicates.no_reason_to_disturb_findings: The record provides no basis for disturbing the concurrent factual findings.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges concurrent possession findings based on evidence and there is no basis to disturb them, the findings are affirmed.
